title: Parashurama's challenge
hookLine: on the road home from the wedding, a man with an axe stops Rama: one avatar of Vishnu meets the next
carry: avatara: the divine comes down, again and again

cards: It should be a caravan of pure joy. King Dasharatha, his four sons, four new daughters-in-law, priests, soldiers and wagons of gifts from King Janaka, all rolling back toward Ayodhya. Then the birds begin to cry harshly.
At the same moment, deer pass by on the right, a good sign. The king is worried, and Vasishtha reads the signs for him: something frightening is coming, and it will pass. A wind rises.
The ground shakes. Dust hides the sun. And out of the dark walks a man with an axe on his shoulder.

teach.h: A FIRE NO ONE CAN LOOK AT.
teach.b: Valmiki describes him like a fire no one can look at straight: matted hair, a bow in one hand, the axe across his shoulder.
He's the son of the sage Jamadagni, of the family of Bhrigu, a brahmin, a priest's son, who took up weapons.
After his father was killed in a feud with a royal house, the stories say, he made war on the warrior class again and again. Later tradition calls him Parashurama, Rama with the axe.
Now he has heard that a young prince broke Shiva's great bow, so he's brought a bow of his own, and a story. Long ago, he says, the divine craftsman made two bows, one for Shiva and one for Vishnu.
In his telling, a contest broke out, and one roar from Vishnu left Shiva's bow slack. Shiva's bow passed to the kings of Videha; that's the one Rama broke.
Vishnu's bow came down through Parashurama's family, and here it is.

teach.h: STRING THIS ONE, THEN WE FIGHT.
teach.b: String this one, he tells Rama, and then we fight. Dasharatha begs; Parashurama doesn't even answer him. Here is what Hindus see on this road.
The word is avatara, a coming down. Hindus count ten great descents of Vishnu, the Dashavatara, and in most lists Parashurama is the sixth and Rama the seventh. Why come down at all?
In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna, another avatar, gives the reason: whenever dharma falls and wrong rises, I come, age after age, to protect the good and set dharma back on its feet.
So on a dusty road home from a wedding, one Rama faces another, and in the tradition's eyes, both are Vishnu.

how: Hindu tradition counts Parashurama among Vishnu's ten avatars, the Dashavatara, usually listed sixth after the man-lion and the dwarf and before Rama; his birth is marked on Parashurama Jayanti in the spring month of Vaishakha.

games.q: Sam asks why Vishnu keeps coming down in new forms. by what Krishna says in the Gita, what's the reason?
o: whenever dharma falls, to protect the good and set dharma right.
to compete with the other gods for worship.
only once, at the start of the world, and never again.
games.why: in the Gita, Krishna says he comes age after age whenever dharma declines. that's avatara: on this road, the sixth avatar meets the seventh.

practice: If you pray, say softly on each breath out, om namo narayanaya, a prayer to Vishnu, the one who keeps coming down when he's needed. Let the words slow you.
If you don't pray, breathe out slowly and picture the wedding party on that road, everyone still, waiting to see what the young prince will do.

wordCard.voice: Parashurama's challenge. Rama with the axe, counted the sixth avatar, meets Rama the seventh and holds out Vishnu's bow: string it, and then we fight.

orig.note: Sanskrit paraśurāma: Rama with the paraśu, the axe. Valmiki mostly calls him Jamadagnya, son of Jamadagni.

carryVoice: Your line: avatara, the divine comes down, again and again. Tomorrow, Rama answers. That's day five hundred twelve.
